div1.head: Interview with Robert E. Emerson, Jr. [11/25/2002]

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Robert E. Emerson, Jr. Mr. Emerson served in the U.S. Army, in the European theater. I am Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Emerson's home in Garfield Heights, Ohio, on November 25th, 2002. Robert was 83 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: 1941, I was living in Garfield Heights, not on this street; but I was on Wadsworth Avenue, just opposite the -- well, what is now the shopping center, but back then was the Smith Brothers farm. So it was -- goes back a few years. I would say probably 1926 is when we moved out here, and I was seven years old at that time. So that's where I was raised, and that's where I was at the time when con- -- conscription, I'll say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or you can say the "draft."

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Well, the draft, yeah. See, sometimes the brain doesn't want to function. I was interested in horsemanship and things. I worked out at a little riding academy here called the "B Bar B." And I decided I didn't want to be a foot slogger, so I signed in for the cavalry at -- in here in Cleveland, the 107th Cavalry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I signed up.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: No, no, no. I went in and signed up. In fact, to my memory here, I think it was the -- let me see. It says "Date of Enlistment, 13 February '41."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And we were -- went into active service in March of that same year. We left Cleveland. Well, I say we -- we practiced in Cleveland. Cleveland was known as the "Black Horse Troop" for the 107th. Cincinnati was, I think -- I don't know which one -- Cincinnati or Columbus were bays, and one was chestnuts. That's the way they had all the horses -- were color-coded, if you want to call it that. Headquarters was here in Cleveland. And then, as I say, after we were -- went into the federal service, we moved from Cleveland to Tullahoma, Tennessee. That was Camp Forrest at that time, named after General Forrest, of course. And there was not much at Camp Forrest, believe me. We wound up cutting down trees and clearing areas for parade grounds and everything else. Of course, we had our stables, and that was pretty much that, and that was our -- And then from Camp Forrest, we went to Louisiana Maneuvers back then, and we had quite a -- what can I say? We had a lot of interesting things happen to us. We camped out, just as we would; and it was amazing. Things I remember was, of course, during maneuvers, we ran circles around the tank corps in the Louisiana swamp area because we could move, and they couldn't. I spent a lot of my time in the States. Out of five years, I spent one year overseas, so most of my memory is from stateside. After we went there, we went to Fort Oglethorpe in Georgia, and I don't remember where we went after that. But anyhow, during the time of -- we spent -- we were on the western -- we spent -- practiced, you know, with the horses and everything. One of the things I did was help break horses. We did hunter trials and things like they do in the horse shows today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What exactly would be a hunter trial ___+?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Well, it would be a laid out area, and you would have to jump and go over water and long jumps of that type, you know. It was -- for me, it was interesting, because this is what I wanted. I had been -- I rode more the way -- the western style on what is known as a "stock saddle." And, of course, when I got in the service, it was English and -- not English. It was a military-type saddle, and -- however, they used the English method of riding. So when we would go out on a column or something like that, I would probably catch hell most of the time. I worked with long stirrups. I did not like this business of bouncing up and down in the saddle, like the English do, so I rode like cowboys. When they went into a trot, I kind of stood up and just let him go, and I would get -- a lot of times, I would get called out, you know, "Kick that horse into a trot," or, "Post, post." Well, okay. I'll post, you know. As soon as the officer would leave, I would kick him back into what I wanted, and I would ride my easy chair. That's what it amounted to. And then we went from camp, here. I'm trying -- I can't think of the date when we actually left Tennessee, but we were supposed to go -- my understanding was that we were supposed to go overseas. In fact, we left camp after December 7th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what camp? Where were you exactly on December 7th?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Tullahoma at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Because I know I was supposed to be on furlough; and when I left, I was walking out of the barracks. And my officer was -- his office was in our barracks; and he wanted to see my discharge -- my travel papers because he didn't -- he said he wasn't sure that he had signed them. And he looked at my papers and ripped them in half. And I -- of course, I hit the ceiling. And he said, "Well, didn't you hear the radio say about Pearl Harbor?" And I said, "Yeah. But where the hell is Pearl Harbor?" You know, I've got nothing about that. I found out in a hurry. And it was shortly after that, that we were scheduled to go. And I -- I don't want to lie about it, but I think they said that when we hit California, we would be embarked for the Philippines, which was a bad place to go. And Reno, Nevada, on the way down there, we threw a wheel on the engine that was taking the troop train, and, of course, so we stopped. We landed -- I think it was about three o'clock, four o'clock in the morning, in San Francisco. And they had picked up another CAB outfit, a recon outfit, and shipped them over, because the ship was leaving. The convoy was leaving at midnight. So from that time on, we were on what is known as the "Western Defense Command." And we had a lot of training, you might say. We trained -- first of all, we had the horses for two years, to begin with. And when we got out to California, we did a lot of riding out there, and that's where they decided they were going to take the horses away and give us Jeeps and armored cars. Well, when we got the Jeeps and the armored cars, we took them out in the dessert and decided to see how well they would do against horses. Of course, there were a lot of Jeeps that were turned over and armored cars that wouldn't go up dunes very well, and we got sat down. The colonel said, "You guys can't drive? You'll walk." And that's what we did. I remember the motorcycle guys, when they got the bikes, you know, they were -- man, they were doing handstands and everything else, going down the company street, so that was quit. Now, then, we had -- we were on Western Defense Command. We -- pretty much from San Francisco north, we patrolled. In those days you had blackouts and everything else, so we would have to patrol along -- mostly, I would -- my group was up around Eureka, California. And we went from there to the south, and then we went north to the California border. I was in communications, but we had to make our patrol, too, so... And we sprung -- strung wire up and down telephone poles, climbing, you know. We didn't have buckets and that kind of thing. You put spikes on and went up the pole. And we had some nice, interesting things going on. We had to be very careful about falling off the pole. I can recall one day, down on the beach, that I was -- at that time I was sergeant of communications, and I was up a pole. And what we would do is go up a pole, two people; and you would hopscotch from one pole to the next. And just as I released my safety belt, I said to my partner, "Be careful when you take the belt off, because these poles are hard, and you don't want to drop." And I no sooner said it, and I landed on my back, on the beach, which was about a 20-, 30-foot drop. The gentleman who was on the other pole looked down at me and says, "What did you say, Sarge? I didn't hear that." Well, I told him what I had said but not the way I had originally said it. But, no, he was -- we did this kind of thing. We did a lot of -- during storms and things, we had to run wire and repair. And I can remember one time we went all the way up to the border, where they had a Coast Guard station. And they were tied in to our little net, you might say. And we couldn't find a break in the wire. We couldn't find anything. We got to the Coast Guard station and found that the wire went in through the window, and some nice swabbie had slammed the window down on the wire, and that's where the break was. And it was -- you know, in California the winters are wet, and it was cold and miserable, and it was storming. And two of us made the trip, pole by pole, until we found where the break was. So it was -- what? -- about two years, a little over two years, that we were in California.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any scares? Any thoughts or rumors that the Japanese were close to the coast?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. We -- we sent a -- up near -- I can't think of the damn town in California. It's near the border up there -- Crescent City.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: They had a sub scare. And, of course, we sent a group up with a tow -- 37-millimeter. I mean, you know, what are we going to do? So they did fire at it, and I don't know whether they ever hit it or not, but it disappeared. And I understand that down along Los Angeles, they did get one down there that had come in. But because we were a communication unit that I was with, out at Eureka, one of the things in Eureka, we had a 110-foot pole that we used for an antenna. We had -- Western Electric had put it up for us, and we ran wire from there to one of the buildings. We were in an old abandoned school building. And I remember going up the pole one time to put wire, and we did not have handholds. We used climbers. And across the street, a young lady opened the window, and she says, "Be careful up there." She said, "I under- -- you realize that there's a picket fence down below you?" And right against the pole was an iron picket fence, which we never thought of until she mentioned it. Yeah. We had some -- in the States we had some things that -- on patrol we -- at night patrol we had -- I can remember one time we had a semi going up Highway 1 -- which was the coastal highway -- with his lights on. And we tried to slow him down, and he got very upset. And we moved the armored car in front of him, and the guy running the turret swung the 37-millimeter and asked him if he really wanted to stop. And I think he did. And one of the guys -- one of the gentlemen got out at that point and fixed the headlights. So he had to use his -- we call them "cats' eyes." But he was not a happy man. But, you know, the thing was, we were -- on Highway 1 you were a sitting duck for something coming up out of the ocean. And here's a guy driving his headlights, and he was a sitting target. And we worked with the police departments and things like that. But the big antenna we had up there, we got some guys come in one day, civies, civilian clothes, and walked into the communications room. It's a wonder they didn't get shot, because the gentleman in the communication room had a hub -- stub -- submachine gun as his weapon, and he invited them out. And we finally found out that they were med -- Federal Communications. They said that our transmissions were going out over the ocean. We were too powerful. What we had done, a doctor in town had a ham setup. He had a five-tier ham operating thing. And my repair boy, he was pretty good on this stuff, and he rigged the whole thing up to the communication circuit, the military, because they moved it where -- where we were, and we were not allowed to use it. However, I did prove to them that by taking the whip on the armored car, I could reach San Francisco across the mountains just as good as I could with the thing. I says, "What difference does it make, you know, actually?" But we were probably putting out enough power, they said, at the point raised that we were -- on the meter we were flipping the meter up against the end. So we had to cut it back. Then we went to Texas; Camp Hood, Texas, in way -- outside of Waco, a place called "Gatesville." I understand that they have a big federal prison down there now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: When we were there, it was absolutely nothing. We used to call it "Goatsville," because that's what it was. It was a little flat. It was -- they called it a town, but there was nothing. You could probably drive through it in two minutes, you know. But my wife, she had a room down there, a house. I tell you how they rented houses for soldiers. This woman had a five-room house. She slept in the hall, and she had five families living in the house, and they had to share kitchen -- kitchen privileges and things. So then finally when they said we were moving, she went -- put her on a train and brought her back to Cleveland. We went to New York. So that would have been '45. New Year's Eve, my buddy and I had a pass to go to New York. Now, you had two choices. You could get a pass in the afternoon, or you could get an evening pass. Well, we opted for the evening, you know, I mean, New York, I mean, man, New Year's Eve. So about four o'clock, we got the word, "Pack up. Get ready." And we've done this so often in the -- in the first four years. It seemed like every time we turned around, we were either packing or unpacking. And so we packed our stuff. And I understand that the MPs went out to New York and started picking up boys in uniform, bringing them back. Well, I will never forget that, because when we board -- boarded ship, we went through a line. And I think, if I can remember rightly, there were medics, two medics, on each -- it was a medic on each side of the line, and there were six medics. Anyhow, you went through the line. I got banged on both sides, each one, so we -- I got at least six shots before we boarded ship. When we boarded ship, we were sitting out there. When we moved, we started going past the statue. You could hear the bells and the whistles from New York. We went out at midnight. For some reason they always wanted moved at midnight. 16 days, landed in Le Havre. We were the first ship into the cleared harbor at Le Havre, France, and we wound up at a place called "Camp Lucky Strike." I don't know if you know what a recon unit was like. We had Jeeps. We had -- not tanks. We had armored cars, with little 37-millimeter guns on them. And after we got to Le Havre, we went to Camp Lucky Strike, and we -- I don't know how long we were there, but we were supposed to go to the Bulge. And we were lined up when a motorcycle guy came up and handed a message to the commander. And he told us to disembark, that we weren't going. Now, what had happened, my understanding was that the second ship in had a tank unit on board. So they were lucky. They got to go to the Bulge because they were a tank unit. But our stay at Lucky Strike was, again, interesting because we -- we had quite a good stay there. And the boys, some of the guys, found out that calvados -- calvados was the local drink. And I can remember one time when -- where one of the guys came in, and -- I don't know how to explain the taste of calvados. It was -- I put one shot in a pint of coffee, and after the gentleman that passed it around to us left, I threw the coffee out, to give you an idea what it was like. Anyhow, this gentleman -- this boy comes home, into the tent. The fire is almost out. So he's got about two or three inches of calvados in the bottle. And he -- instead of pouring it in, he's just going to throw the damn bottle and let it break in, you know, these potbellied stoves.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Well, he did. We lost the tent, the stove, everything else. So, you know, I mean, little things like that. One of the troop guys, not ours, but he -- he did tell us one day that -- you know, we're still fighting the Germans. And after a couple of days, this one guy gets suspicial (sic) about -- suspicious -- You know something?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Suspicious.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. You can't understand. It's been about, I don't know, how many years now that I had a stroke; and every once in a while, this comes back on me. He saw this fellow, and he didn't know him -- so he -- going through the mess line. So finally he had called one of the MPs over and says, "You know, you better find out what outfit he's from." Well, they find out that he's not from any outfit. He's a German officer in fatigues that was using our -- he didn't want to fight. He was -- he was there getting his lunch and breakfast and everything else, but that's at that time. Then, of course, we went to -- we were sent to Saint-Nazaire, France. Now, we were not at Saint-Nazaire. Saint-Nazaire is a port city, and we were on the perimeter. We had a fairly good-sized detachment of Germans that were holding Saint-Nazaire. They couldn't come out. We couldn't go in -- or we wouldn't go in. We just figured that -- I guess, that we're going to sit there and let them starve until they decided to give up. So from my own standpoint, at that point, I was notified that because of the -- my communications, supposed, skills, I was going to be transferred. And at that point they sent me to the 106th Regiment, and -- or was it the 106th? It was an Army division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think it was the 106th Division.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: 106th. In other words, we were -- no -- yeah. I guess it was, because I've got a paper from one of the officers. I copied this, the 29th Mechanized Cavalry Reconnaissance Troop. So the hundred -- 29th Mechanized had to be part of the 106th Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That makes sense.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And the division was -- what we always called it -- the "Golden Lion," because that's the patch we had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And at -- prior to my transfer, my -- my -- oh, God. Prior to my transfer, my combat time was at Saint-Nazaire. They've got here -- yeah -- "France GO 33 & 40 WD 45, Battles and Campaigns."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: They give you these American service -- I never sent for them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't? You should.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: No. I don't even have the -- I don't even have the -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Ruptured Duck or whatever you --

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: What do you call them? Ribbons.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, any ribbons. You didn't get those ribbons?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: No. I don't have any ribbons. The only thing I've got is a pair of -- I think I got them down in the basement someplace -- a pair of staff sergeant things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't automatically send this to you? You have to request it?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These medals, they didn't just give them to you?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, no. You have the ribbon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And my understanding is that you've got to -- you got to send for them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: According to that, I have three ribbons -- four, because I have the Bronze Star.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You could get all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. But what am I -- at my age I'm not going to -- come on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You deserve it.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pretty hanging on the wall.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. But, no, here, just to make sure that I'm right, the date of departure, they say here, was January '45, January 3rd. I don't remember that. I remember we went out New Year's Eve, so... And these -- I know I was over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They also say it only took seven days, date of arrival, so...

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, that's right. I'm sorry. I'm thinking the 16th of January, when I came back here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm. So the trip over --

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- did it take 16 days or 17 days? Do you remember? I mean, I've heard --

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I think it was 16, it seems to me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard -- unless it was one of the fast ocean liners, 16 is what I heard.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: It was a --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- Victory ship -- or a Liberty ship, rather?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: No, no, no. It was a -- it was -- was it Swedish?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I think it was a Swedish cruise ship that we were on, because there was only 5,000 of us on board, roughly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's about the size my dad went over on too.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. But I recall going a lot more than seven days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think that's -- you're right.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And -- because we had seven -- we had -- I remember coming -- they had -- I remember coming back, 16 days. Because, here, according to this we returned here --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- the 16th of January.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And it took -- according to that, it took 13 days to come back.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Right. So I -- somebody goofed up on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm sure that, you know, the clerks --

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- typed in the wrong date.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Because, no, date of departure was New Year's Eve.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And it was New Year's Eve. I remember it was New Year's Eve when we left Bremerhaven, Germany, to come back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: See, when I was over there, when I went to the 106th, I spent part of my time at Eupen, Belgium. The Army had taken the whole town as a R&R. Every business, like this town hall, had a GI in charge. Every hotel had at least one GI in charge, every small business. Now, my buddy -- I think I got a picture of Brownie in here. My buddy had -- he had a cafe a couple doors away from where I was, and I had what was called a "Klosterstuble." That was the Kloster family. They had a bar, cafe, and a restaurant. I was responsible for feeding, I think it was, 50 civilians, that worked for the government, lunch every day. And that meant that I had to bring in supplies. And the lady and husband that owned the place were very nice. They -- I ate with them in the kitchen. And their sister-in-law, I think it was, ran the bar. And I had three girls as waitresses, and they did the cleaning up too. It was very interesting. The one thing, these were hand-crank generators. You had to crank them in order to work. Now, one guy would crank them, and the other one would use the key, because this was not voice. This was keyed communications.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Morse code?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Morse code -- dit, dash -- yeah, which we used to do on horseback, moving. We had a crew of -- we had the operator. You had the guy reading -- leading the pack horse. You had one fellow cranking, and two rice -- riflemen. That was your five-man crew that you worked with. At this point in time, it was not Black Horse. This was the C-Troop. I was with C-Troop at that point. I had been transferred from one place to another because they wanted radio operators.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Let's get back to Europe, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What was your job with the 106th? That same thing? Recon?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: It was a recon. Now, the 106th. The reason we were transferred is, the 106th had been in the Bulge. They got pretty well beat up. So they were picking people up from various units and trying to rebuild, I guess, the 106th. I fought it as much as I could. I went as far as the executive officer of the troop before they would transfer me, because, like I said, I had been with the troop for over four years, and I wanted to finish my time with the 107th, too, and because we always felt the 107th was a prestige outfit -- you know what I mean? -- regardless of what other people think, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And I still belong to the Cleveland Cavalry Club, which is the remnants of the 107th; and we have meetings twice a year; and they now take in the active members, you know, because of how many of us are left. But then from there, we went to -- when we went to Eupen -- oipen (ph) is the proper pronunciation -- like I said, I had charge of a restaurant, and Brownie had charge of a bar, and it was pretty nice. The people enjoyed having Americans there. When we got ready to leave, they were very -- the people of Eupen were very unhappy because the British were coming back in; and, for some reason, they didn't cotton too much to the British. So where did we go? Now I can't tell you. Now we were stuck in little towns here and there in Germany. We -- oh, we had to convoy through different places. I don't remember. I slept through the convoy when it went through Paris. Lucky me. We went through these -- some of these little Deutsches, you know, that are some beautiful counties up in the hills and so forth. But, again, I can't tell you which ones we were in. Now, at that time Brownie and I were both artists. I have a couple of paintings that I made over there. When I left Eupen, I go -- gave all my equipment to Brownie because he was staying. And I don't know whether he stayed permanently or what, but he was -- he enjoyed Belgium, and, well, it was one of these things. I mean, we -- When we were at -- I know I'm digressing -- but when we went -- were at -- you asked whether we had any -- any problems or any scary things. Okay. Yeah. At Saint-Nazaire they had a -- the Germans had a railroad gun. Now, it was so -- set up so that the town we were in, their gun was a -- what was it? It was what they called an "88," I guess. Yeah. It was a railroad gun. But it would fire only down the street, the main street.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: That was the only -- apparently, the only place they had it set up for. And I can remember, you know, standing. We never went -- walked in the middle of the road, on the edge, because you never knew when one was coming. And my partner over there, a fellow from Chicago, he had nerves of steel. He was one of these fellows that, "If it's going to happen, it's going to happen. There's nothing I could do about it." He walked down, cleaning his musket, "Oh, look at that." And you could see the swirl coming up off the -- the -- of dust. The thing it would usually hit down at the end of the street -- and there was a big church down there, and it would kind of batter on that. And one time, by myself, I was out stringing wire, and I got pinned down. My buddy came out, wanted to know why I was laying in the mud. And I said, well, there was a sniper out there and that he was getting kind of close. "Well, oh, yeah," he said, "I can see him." And he unlimbered his rifle and took a shot at him, and the guy disappeared. He didn't hit him, but, I mean, he was -- in the meantime, my buddy says, "Come on. Let's get out of here." So we took off. And when I went to the 106th, I -- I don't remember doing too much of anything, because by that time things were winding down. In fact, the war was over when I was at Eupen, Belgium.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And one of the reasons why we were shipped in, they went home, and a number of people from different outfits -- I was all packed up, ready to come home. And my outfit was on trucks and everything, ready to go. And my first sergeant come over, and he said, "What are you packed up for?" And I said, "Well, we're leaving." He says, "Yeah. But you're not." Crazy situation, they had a thing going. Certain people were what they called "essential." Because of the radio speed and the years that I had spent with the communications, I was now essential. And I couldn't figure that out. If the -- if the war was over with, why -- how could you be essential? you know. But anyhow, they had units there that were taking up the slack, and, you know, that was it, you know. So I'm stuck there. Then I got sent, and I really don't know who I was sent with. It was one outfit I was with at that point. We went to Bremerhaven. And then from Bremerhaven, we came back here. When going over, the only thing I remember is, we were chased by a submarine for a while; and we watched the destroyers shoot depth bombs, you know. Coming back, the only thing that happened coming back was that we came -- because it was January, we came through the North Sea at the worst time of the year, in the worst storm that they had had. We made -- and I'll have to use it in knots -- we made 24 knots in 24 hours. That's -- so you -- you went 25 miles in 24 hours. I can remember being on the bow of the ship, and we were crazy, because we were -- you would look up at the sky; and the next thing you look, you would be looking at the bottom of the ocean. And the Marines came out and rousted us back into the ship. The interior of the ship was not the place to be, actually, because you were so crowded coming out. We were coming back. Now, I know my story is kind of disjointed; but as I pop things up, I can think of them. But my most enjoyment -- enjoyable part -- time was when I was with the horse troops. And, of course, like this, here, was, I told you, the Pogonip Country Club out in California.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you part of the occupied forces in Germany?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Well, we went in -- well, a year. We were a full year --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the people?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- to the day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: You know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the German people?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Got along with the German people okay. You would just -- we would do -- surround a small village or something, because they were having problems with contraband, weapons -- what else? -- cigarettes, and all that. Cigarettes were better than money over there at the -- and I didn't smoke at the time. So my cigarettes, I used to pass them out to the guys, you know, "Hey, you got any cigarettes? I'm going into town," you know. But we would make surprise raids on a -- on a circle or town or something like that, and then we would go door to door, and, I mean, really go in and search. And I can remember one time embarrassing -- actually, embarrassing to me. We went into this house, went in through room by room, and opened drawers and things, and walked into this one room. This girl is in bed, and she wouldn't get up. So one of the guys went over and grabbed the blanket and flipped it, and she is totally naked, and she was very unhappy. And I told her, you know, "Well, too bad," got her out of bed and got her -- you know, checked under the pillow and everything, opened the dresser, found a whole stash of cartons of cigarettes. Well, that was confiscated. What we really were looking for was weapons. In a couple of the houses, I think they did find maybe a pistol, something like that, no major weapons. The thing you had to watch -- this was after the war. During the wartime you had to even watch the kids, because they would slip up and throw a grenade underneath a car or something. You know, these were kids. You know, an American soldier with a kid, you know, hey, 10, 12 years old, you know, give them candy or anything like that, and they would blow you up. That's the way they were raised. We didn't have too many of those problems. Most of our problems were being rousted out at two o'clock in the morning to make a raid someplace. We actually got along pretty well. Now, I know in Belgium, they didn't consider themselves German. You know what I mean? But they were the enemy. A good example would be this Klosterstuble, the place I was in charge of -- How did I miss this? We first went in there -- for the GIs, we only had one place that we could shower. Now, I was -- I lived on the second -- like a third floor, almost. They had a room for me. They always called us "chef," the chief of the house, you know. And without thinking, I threw my rifle on the bed, sidearm, went down, grabbed my stuff, was going to take a shower. (END OF DISC ONE; BEGIN DISC TWO.)

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: We had just come in from a pretty good road trip, and this was when we first got there, you know. And the one girl, it was her job to make up the bed and clean up everything. Well, I was down in the shower. About the time I got done, you know, oh, my God, I left my rifle and pistol laying on the -- you know, all my armament. I sailed back to that place and walked in, never said anything to anyone upstairs, you know. Everything was laid out, beautiful, cleaned. It was cleaned better than I ever cleaned it, polished. Every bit of what ammunition I had was there. My rifle was clean. My boots were polished. Everything was hung up. And I'm like, holy, mackerel. And then she was -- apologized because it wasn't a good room. Yeah. Oh, well. This family, the Klosters -- I found one thing in Germany: They start teaching the kids -- at that time, anyhow, they taught them English from the first grade on. Their son was a third-grader, I think; and he was still -- he was only seven years old at that time; but he worked. He was my interpreter. Now, the people that owned the place -- of course, we had to bring in the food for everything and check. And she -- though she spoke English, some, not much, she's going to teach me German. And she would not talk to me in English, and we're trying to get a case of cabbages, to make meals, you know. And she's giving me all these names in German, and I'm trying to check them off on a list that the truck had left me, and I was going crazy. Now, at that point I did speak a little German, very little, because my parents -- my grandparents were German. In fact, I was only about 80 miles from the ancestral home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: But they would not let me go to see it. They had -- they let a couple guys go, and they got into trouble. The one kid, he came back. He was Steven. He was -- his uncle -- and he says he was ready to shoot him because he was a diehard Nazi. And, of course, this was after the war. And so they canceled all visitations to family, if you had family there. But I will say that my study of Latin in high school helped in France because I was able to -- maybe not communicate too well, but I could understand. And you could learn the French method of buying something, how much do you pay? you know. And a couple times got -- I called -- caught people that were telling us something costs so much, and, "Oh, just give us four francs," you know. Yeah. It was worth about one. And in Germany I got to a point where I could speak, because I listened to my grandparents at home and everything. But at one of the USOs, they had a woman that was checking GIs in, you know, when they came. And I spoke to her in German. And she looked at me, and she wanted to know what I was doing in an American uniform. And I said, "Now, wait a minute," you know, "I can speak, but slowly." She says -- I forget what area it was, but she says, "You speak from this area, the inflection that you would use." And I said, "No. I don't know," you know. But people, yeah, we got along. It was the holiday time, and I remember this young woman with a little girl, and she was, you know -- these kids from -- you know, kids, so... And I had gone into a little store, and I got a little doll, and I saw her walking in the square, and I asked the mother whether I could give the little girl the doll. Oh, yeah. Hey, I wound up having a meal with the little girl and the mother and their -- her mother and father, you know, and it was nice. Yeah. There were those that I always kept my hand on my gun, and there were others that were just very nice people. The people in Belgium, I had no -- nothing at all. A couple of the little towns we were in, yeah, I can remember one night, because I ran the projector for the movies. And these guys all took off, and I've got about a half-mile walk back to camp, and it's pitch-black. They don't have streetlights. And I'm walking, and I hear {tapping sound}. Yeah. I stop. It stops. I start. It starts. I stop. Okay. I had the .45 stuck in my belt, because we were not allowed to use them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And I took it out, and I -- {clicking sound} -- and I said in German, "Stop following me." And I started to walk away, and it was totally quiet. So whoever it was, was probably just as scared and was following somebody home because they didn't want to be out there by themselves. But when I got back, I told the lieutenant. I says, "Don't ever let me sit up there at that theater" -- whatever they were using for the shows -- "alone," because we were having trouble with the projector, and I had to carry that damn projector back and the film and everything and then take it back to the headquarters the next day. Little things like that, which -- Brownie and I would go out, and we would pent -- paint. I've got one of the little towns that we were at, you know, and things like that, and it was -- yeah. How do they say it? I wouldn't give you two cents to do it over, and I wouldn't give you a million dollars for the experience, but it's -- it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much entertainment? Any USO shows? Anything like that?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: We didn't, really. As a recon unit, we were pretty much on the outskirts of everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I don't remember ever seeing a show like they show on TV and things like that, no. I don't remember that. We were always in the boondocks. Our thing was, as a recon, you're the first in, and you're the last out, you know. So we were always -- if headquarters was here in the middle of the city, we were in some little boondock on the -- on the perimeter --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- that, you know, we never got that much. Here in the States, when they -- not in the States -- when they transferred us -- me from 107th to the 106th, I -- we were -- set up a radio school for -- because they -- they -- that unit had been pretty well decimated during the Bulge, and so we had to train people and, you know, things of that sort. So we were always busy doing something. But like I said, I wouldn't have stayed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I would have liked to have gone back and seen the place, because I remember the people that I was with, not the GIs, but I mean, the civilians. I would like to see what Eupen looks like now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned Brownie. Did you have other close buddies?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, the sergeant, the one that's on the horse, and Porter and Brownie. And I was -- I was going to -- there's a little one here, someplace. He was small. He became a lieutenant, eventually. This is in the States, now. We were out in the Mojave Desert. And his name was Brownson, Sergeant Brownson. He always said that the only reason he got in was, he hit himself with a hammer or something, raised a bump on his head so that he would pass the height requirement. I mean, he was small. And he was one of our friends. And Brownie was about the -- of course, Brownie was with -- I met him through the 106th. He wasn't with the 107th, see. And, yeah, we had friends, Harris, Sergeant Harris is one. He wound up as an officer and went to the Philippines and got killed. A number of our guys had finally gone over, you know. And, oh, what the hell is his name? Merv Jensen, he was the one from Chicago. In fact, I came back home and got married, and I was the first man married in our church, in uniform. So we were married in '42. And when I came back to camp, Merv was heading out of the room. I was in the orderly room at the time, and we were talking, and he got up, and he walked out, you know. He was answering the telephone and that. And he's almost past the barracks. He said, "By the way, Bob, your wife is here." And he takes off. He met my wife when she came to California. And I had to stay -- I had to grab somebody to stay in the orderly room so that I could get out, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And we found a small place for her to stay. And the people we were -- one of them was in -- oh, God. See, I got Eureka on the brain again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- Palau Island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And my wife would come home. And then she immediately got sick, wound up in the hospital. And she got a job with one of the top doctors in California. He took care of her, but -- and we've had friends from there that we -- they still send us cards, and we send them cards, you know. Never got back there. But overseas, I mean, yeah, the people were -- I'm sorry. The people that I met were okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Now, the guys from 106th that were, of course, in the Bulge and -- and everything else, they were -- they were really dead-set against the Germans, and I had to keep my mouth shut. Don't forget, my grandparents came from Germany. I mean, they -- she came here when she was 16 years old, you know, but even so -- And when we were in France, the one thing I found out, the French were very friendly. They were our enemies, to begin with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: So -- but we found in little towns that we were in -- I don't remember really going to a large city, except Bremerhaven, when we were ready to go -- leave, you know. But the little towns we were in were kind of like agricultural things. I do remember being on patrols before I got there into Belgium. We would listen for shells coming in and things of that -- you know, or -- or mortars, especially. When we were at Saint-Nazaire, they had -- the Germans would pull something that they would -- we would have three groups; and maybe this group is firing a mortar; and the minute you fired it, they would fire at this group. And then this group would bellyache about the fact that we're shooting at them. They were very -- very sneaky in that way, things like that, you know. And, well, I'll give you an idea. Our mortar pit was outside the -- the door of this house we were in. Of course, those houses in France are built out of stone, and they're about two foot thick, you know. So the mortar pit was about 10, 15 foot away from the back door.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And we had the thing set up where we thought that -- that German village was in Saint-Nazaire, you know. You take one and get the thing, open the door, out, drop it, and never stop. I had figured out that I could go around this thing here, drop the shell here. I could be back in before it landed over there. I was one of the fastest guys in the group. We were in an observation post at this troop, a church that we were at. And I don't know how they managed to get a big one, but they -- you could hear it. You knew it was coming in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And I was up there, taking care of the telephone; and the guy -- was Eric, I guess his name was -- was the other sergeant that was up there, and he says, "Incoming." Well, we're on the third floor of this tower. I dropped my rifle, picked it up, dropped my tools. I'm now trying to get down the stairs; right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I must have done that two or three times and beat the other crew down into the basement. And he -- one of the fellows had a -- where they used to dump hay down. He had a big pile of hay. He just stepped off, down into the pile of hay. But it was -- like I say, it's interesting. Every once in a while, something will pop into your head, and you'll remember, you know. But to put it in chronological order, there was no -- no way. But I do remember when we were still horse troops and in maneuvers and things of that sort. You have, no doubt, heard about the Louisiana Maneuvers. That was the big one. We were told, at that time, that a machine gunner in a mounted unit had a life expect- -- life expectancy of three minutes. You stop to figure that a .30 caliber gun -- these are water-cooled guns -- on a pack saddle -- now he's got to stop that horse, get off his horse, unlimber the gun, and set it up to a position where he could work, you know. I was going to tell you something else. This one here, one of the horses, out in California, dropped into a ravine. He was -- we were out in -- near a little California town in the mountains. That's when he lost the horse. They had to bring an ambulance out. We finally managed to get the horse up on its feet and up. So I was staying with the lame horse. And they put him in the ambulance, and they were going to take him back to town. And, God, I wish I could think of the name of the town, because it's a big place. I'll think of it eventually. They said -- well, this is at night, now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I did not have a rifle. This is mountain lion area, and that they had told us a couple days before the -- the guide had gotten one. He says it was about nine foot from tip to tail, so it's a big bird -- animal. So I'm going to stay with the horse, the lame horse. And they're going to drive slow enough that I can follow the ambulance, because I don't know where I'm at.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: All of a sudden, they decided to take off. And there I am, in the mountains, with a lame horse. I have a .45 on my belt, and I'm concerned. I got to get the -- because I don't know where I'm going. So I'm looking, and I see this road curves way down the mountain. Oh, to hell, we'll go through the field, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I'm going through the field, and all of a sudden I look, and one of these bulls had spotted us. And he came -- come, head down, and, I mean, he is coming, you know. I put the stirs in to hold the horse. And finally, I let go of the lead grain, and I said, "You're on your own, baby." And we finally get to a fence. Well, this horse was limping like crazy, going -- {Telephone rings.}

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Where was I?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Talking about --

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, in California, yeah. Well, you said you wanted -- wanted some of the things that happened, yeah. And believe me, when we cleared that fence, that lame horse was right alongside of me, and she wasn't limping. And that damn bull hit that fence. And, you know, out in California, those are pretty hefty things, and they went for a long time, and I'd seen that thing rattling. And I said, "Well, I'm going to go down, you know, and follow the road." That's what we did, because I didn't know where -- I didn't know where the camp was because they had moved camp when we were out. And I'm going down this hill, and it's dark, and I see something at the base of the tree -- and I thought, oh, boy. You know, I'm very carefully moving. Damn thing jumps up, and it's a cow, you know. So anyhow, I start singing "Home on the Range," and I sang that as loud as I could, because I figured if there's anybody out there, not a person, but an animal, they're going to get out of the way. I don't know. It took me about four hours. In the meantime, I see the lights from the city, and I figured, by God, if I can't find camp, I'm going right into town, and somebody will take pity on me and the horse, you know. But about -- it must have been about four o'clock in the morning, I guess, when I finally hit camp. And they were camped on both sides of this road.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And my lieutenant met me, and he finally said, "Will you shut up." He says, "We have listened to 'Home on the Range' for the last three hours," wake everybody up in camp, because voices travel out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Jeez, it was really -- but I was so tired, and I rolled off that saddle, and he had one of the other guys come take the horses and put them on the picket line.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: One other time we were in Louisiana. They were going someplace, and I -- well, you get off the horse. You sit down. You know, you lay down or something, whatever. I'm laying there with a coat rolled up underneath my head. Something nudges me, and I'm -- "Get away from me." And it nudges me again. Finally, I get up, and I said, "Okay." There's nobody there. The troop is gone. The damn horse had stayed with me. I got up. I said, "Well, okay, buddy," and I took the reins and held them in my hand, and I says, "Take off. You know where you're going. I don't." We're out in the middle of nowhere, you know, and he did, about two hours; and he walked right up to the picket line where he's supposed to be tied up. What's his name? Sergeant come -- he come out. He says, "Where the hell have you been?" "Oh, looking around the swamps." But there's some things that happen. Over a five-year period you forget everything. Sometimes you can remember something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. When they told me they were going to throw me out of the 107th and sent me over to the 106th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bad day.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: That -- that's about -- that, and, like I said, the sniper -- sniper incident.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: As a communications man, I was not supposed to go out on these patrols, and I kept -- every once in a while, we'd keep -- Oh, I didn't tell you one. Yeah. One of the guys was a treasure hunter. He liked to dig around in places, and we found out -- one day he says, "I think I got a spot," he says, and he started digging. The French had -- apparently, had a habit. When the Germans came in, they buried stuff. Well, we dug this up. What he dug up was bottle after bottle of cognac and champagne and all this. And we cleaned it up and put it in this house that we were in. The lieutenant was living with us at that time, and he said, "Okay." So we had out -- dugouts, where people -- like once a week or something like that, he'd take a bottle and go out and give the guys that wanted a drink a drink, you know, and -- because he was mad at us. He always drank scotch, and he was -- we would take a -- each of us would take a little swallow of his scotch and make sure where it was on the bottle and put water in it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: So one day he called us together. There weren't too many of us in that house. You know, we were the headquarters thing. He says, "I don't mind you drinking my scotch," but he said, "I'll be dammed if I'll let you water it down." So he brings in -- I guess the officers had a way of getting it. And he brings in a couple bottles of scotch. He says, "This is for you guys. You leave mine alone." But, yeah, we were going to get new guys in. Another thing I remember. These houses had doors that were about two inches thick, you know, old farmhouses, French farmhouses. And just as they were bringing in a bunch of -- I guess they were draftees, new kids that just came in. We had the door locked, and we got a bombardment of -- what did I say? -- mortar.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Mortar. Mortar.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: This kid, this one kid, with his fingertips, got the edge of that door and damn near ripped it off its hinges to get in. We had to call the medics. They had to take him out in the jacket. He -- he really blew, and he was just a kid, you know. But, I mean, the other kids were scared, yeah; but, I mean, this one was -- he lost it, totally. We had a lot of fellows from the -- here in the States, we had fellows from Kentucky, Western Virginia. We had a couple of guys from Kentucky. They were buddies. Boy, were they drinkers. Out in California we had a couple Indians, boys, that were in the unit. I don't know if they were in our unit or somebody else's. But he got loaded, and he kept the MPs at bay. He had his bayonet, and he was, "Come and get me. You want me? You come and get me." And, of course, what are they going to do? you know. They finally talked him out of it. He was the chief of one of the tribes, but they couldn't handle their liquor. But it's really -- overseas, not too much as far as incidents. Yeah. I had one -- I had a fellow out on an outpost and told him that when I brought his relief -- relief out, we would flick the lights on the Jeep so that he would know who it was. And we flicked the lights on the Jeep, and he shot out the windshield. So we very carefully got back in the Jeep and backed up far enough so we knew that he -- he couldn't hit us where we were and turned around and went back to camp and said, "Well, let him sit there until daylight, and we'll go out and relieve him." Here in the States, we had new kids come in. Again, not -- not saying anything about Kentucky, but this kid was from a little town someplace, a little -- I was out, and he says, "Halt. Who goes there?" Well, okay, "Sergeant Emerson." "Come forward to be recognized." I come forward. "Halt. Who goes there?" Went through the whole thing again. "Come forward to be recognized. Halt." I said, "Wait a minute. Whoa, what's going on here?" He said, "They told me to say 'halt' three times and shoot." And I'm standing next to a screen door. It didn't stand very long, because I'm standing and looking at him. Man, I went through that screen door. They had to send an officer around, keep his attention while somebody else grabbed the rifle. But, you know, I mean, he didn't know. Now, we had another kid, he would stand there and just, like, on the range. And he told us. He says, "Hey," he says, "Easy." He says, "My daddy gave me a .22" -- he says -- "when I was about this tall." And he said, "I had to go out and get squirrels." And he said, "I better -- better not hit them anyplace but in the head because it messed up the meat." They were good, you know. But they had their own way of thinking. I'm glad they weren't with us when I was overseas. But -- no. And overseas the German people, like I said, when we saw them, it was the average -- average -- not the military -- well, in fact, some of the military. We also had a system that we would take -- afterwards they would take prisoners. They would bring them in to where we were, and they would clean up or do things like that. And I'm sitting in the orderly tent, and this fellow comes in. I've got no weapons, I mean, because I'm sitting there. And he's carrying an M3, you know. I -- oh, boy. And he's a prisoner, you know. And he says -- he could speak English, and he says, "Sergeant," he says, "I found this laying on a stump." He says, "I don't know who it belongs to." And it was loaded, you know. Well, my officer found out who it belonged to. But, I mean, they were like that. Well, one thing we found when we went to the compound to pick up maybe eight, ten guys, you know, they were fighting, who would come, because they got fed, you know, and nobody bothered them. We didn't -- none of the guys bothered them. But some in the 107th knew -- but they were -- I mean, the 106th, they were really down on the Germans, because, like I said, they were in the Bulge. I remember my brother to say how bad it was. Of course, he was in medic during the Bulge -- in the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Continue. Where were we?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Like I said, my brother was in the Bulge, and he just come home -- back with an ambulance, and he was telling me how -- how the -- you know, the Red Cross was supposed to be a safe thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And he had turned the ambulance over to the next driver, and the guy started out, to pull out of the way from the medics, and got blown up. So he says that's how it happened; and, of course, he came out of it okay. Funny little things, you know. Germany, you were not allowed to hunt. Well, one of the reasons we were going to -- was going to fight -- hunt was because there at one time, we had -- Oh, I'm sorry. Did I --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: We had -- we lived about a week on corned beef hash, breakfast, lunch, and dinner. And when the supply truck came in, it was loaded with corned beef hash. Well, they almost lost their driver. But Germany had a rule that you didn't hunt their deer. I mean, they're very protective of the deer at that time. And I couldn't figure it out. We're at war with this country, and yet we can't -- you know. But finally, they came along and said that you could send two men out from each unit. You were allowed one deer, if you could get it. Well, we never did get a deer. I -- I went out one day. And you were only allowed -- you're supposed to have three shells and carbine or rifle. We got out there in the woods, and you could hear this "tap, tap, tap, tap, tap." And, oh, my God, some of these guys are out there hunting with BARs and everything else. I came back, and the lieutenant says, "Why are you back here?" I said, "You go out there." But one day we were driving, four guys in a Jeep; and this deer starts across. And one of the guys -- I don't know which one it was -- took a .45 -- not a .45. We were riding in a Jeep. We're going, and he {shooting sound} -- and the thing rolls over. And, oh, my God, are we in trouble, because that was before we were allowed to hunt. Got the deer, got it in the head. So what are we going to do? Can't leave it lay out here. Pulled it out to the road. The driver went over the leg. Put it in the Jeep. Went back. "What are you guys doing?" "Hey, it ran in front of us. We hit it. What do you want us to do?" The guy says, "I couldn't see it suffer." Well, the lieutenant was a hunter; and, boy, he skinned that thing out in nothing flat. But our cook did not know how to cook. They cut the thing in chunks and fried it, and it was like chewing your shoes. I mean, you don't cook venison that way. Little things pop up into your head now and then. But I have often said I would like to go back, just to see what the town looks like now. It's probably very modern and up -- because it was near -- not too far from Brussels, you know, and there is a military cemetery right near there. Like the people -- that gives me another idea. When we were in Eupen -- I forgot where we had to go. But one of the -- one of the officers -- and I don't even remember which one it was anymore. We had to go someplace, and then we crossed over into Holland, which was a no-no. We went in okay. Now how are we going to come out? Every place we could think of had a checkpoint. So the driver says, "I think I know where I can go." He says -- he headed up a hill. And here's these two guys, Dutchmen, with their bicycles. That was their checkpoint. Well, one of us had to lay out on the stretcher, and one of us had your -- checking him out, and the driver is telling these guards, "We got to get him to the hospital." Lieutenant, of course, he's hiding his things. The guy's -- he's going to go like this. They had a telephone or something there. The driver takes off. He says, "Damn, they're not going to catch me with those bicycles." We're back in Belgium, but we had seen the -- that's a -- oh, yeah. We had seen a military cemetery. He wanted to see the cemetery. And on the way back, he said, "Let's go into Holland." Well, Holland was amazing. The streets are clear. They're clean. People are out washing things, you know. And I can remember France was the dirtiest place.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: You think they're more civilized. But people would urinate on the curb, defecate alongside the street in some of the old -- not in the city, I mean, outside, in the countryside. But it was amazing. I don't know. What, if anything, you want to know. I can't think of more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You covered plenty, given me a real viewpoint.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: I mean, it's often -- it's just as things pop up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's always going to be that way. I've never sat down with anybody, unless they're reading it off a script --

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've never sat down with anybody that's going to go chronological.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Because, actually, there's a lot of things that you forget, and I think sometimes you maybe think of things that you think went this particular -- and it was with something else --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's with everybody.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: When I first came in, we were in Shaker Heights.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: That's where the headquarters were. They had a place here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And I had a uniform, not completely, but partially dress uniform; and I was working the stables; and I had boots, my riding boots, riding breeches. And they had a pit that you had to take -- when you clean the stables, you took the -- the manure in a wheelbarrow, and you went out across this pit on a plank and dumped it. Well, I took a wheelbarrow across the plank, dumped it. The wheelbarrow went in. I went in up to my waist, and you can imagine what it was like.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm. Not that much fun.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And I had to go home on the streetcar. Huh, huh, huh, fun, so... I had brought some stuff home, you know, and he gave me the -- you had to have a certificate of -- oh, if you brought home a camera or anything like that, it had to be certified. And this is the guy that certified mine, commanding the 27th. Now, that's a troop --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- 27th Mechanized Troop, 106th Division. I can't give you a regiment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How does a troop compare? Is a troop -- is that smaller than a regiment?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. When I first went in, a regiment consisted of squadron headquarters -- squadron headquarters, A, B, and C Troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm. So a troop might compare to a company, then?

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. All right.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. In the horse troops --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- we had, of course, an obstacle course that you had to follow with, and they had pop-up targets. So when you started out, you had your .45 in your hand, and you had to take this thing, and you had to hit pop-up targets. So you were shooting over, under, behind your horse; and you're doing this at a gallop.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And that was one of the scores that they kept for you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And we still have -- like I say -- belong to the Cleveland Cavalry Association, and we have -- in the fall we usually have an a -- a steak roast, and we have a Christmas party.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: And we're going to have the Christmas party this year at the Coast Guard downtown --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Robert E. Emerson, Jr.
sp.p: -- and see some of the guys, you know. Like I said, the brain doesn't work that good anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're doing good. (END OF DISC TWO)
